summary: Describes an architecture and framework for letting applications talk to middleboxes such as firewalls and address translators. Such devices cannot always handle protocols like SIP or H.323 by looking at packet headers alone, so the framework lets trusted agents help them make decisions.

plainLanguage.summary: Some firewalls and Network Address Translators (NATs) need application-specific information to handle traffic correctly. This RFC describes an architecture in which an in-path agent can ask a middlebox to allow or translate traffic.

questions: how can applications talk to firewalls
what is a middlebox policy decision point
subtitle: An architecture for letting trusted agents coordinate firewall and NAT behavior.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and NATs may need application information that cannot be learned from packet headers alone.
tldr.mechanism: External in-path agents use a proposed MIDCOM protocol to request services from a middlebox, while a policy decision point helps authorize agents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3303 is an Informational architecture; it states that the MIDCOM protocol is yet to be devised and gives protocol requirements in RFC 3304.

facts.label: MIDCOM protocol
facts.value: Yet to be devised in this RFC

today: RFC 3303 is Informational, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The architecture leaves protocol details to future work; RFC 3304 lists protocol requirements.

sections.title: Why Middleboxes Need Application Help
sections.content:
Firewalls and Network Address Translators (NATs) sometimes need application information that is not visible in packet headers. The RFC uses protocols such as SIP and H.323 as examples of applications with dynamic media traffic.

Embedding knowledge of many applications inside each middlebox can make it complex and hard to maintain. MIDCOM proposes moving that application knowledge to external agents, leaving the middlebox to provide services such as firewall filtering and address translation.
sections.plainLanguage: A middlebox may not recognize the traffic an application will create. An external agent that understands the application can tell the middlebox which traffic to handle.

sections.title: Agents, Policy, and Middleboxes
sections.content:
A MIDCOM agent performs application-level gateway functions while remaining logically external to a middlebox. The RFC considers in-path agents: their host lies on the path of the packets they need to examine. Proxies, gateways, and end hosts can host agents.

A MIDCOM Policy Decision Point (PDP) holds policy profiles and advises a middlebox about agent authorization. Policy rules combine packet filters with actions such as permitting traffic or creating NAT bindings. Registration provisions an agent's profile before it establishes a MIDCOM session.
sections.plainLanguage: The agent understands application traffic, while the middlebox performs firewall or NAT functions. A policy decision point helps the middlebox decide which agents it trusts.

sections.title: Sessions and the MIDCOM Protocol
sections.content:
The architecture has an interface between agents and middleboxes and a separate policy interface to the PDP. The MIDCOM protocol is client-server and initiated by the agent. A session has setup, run-time, and termination phases, and either party or the PDP may cause it to end.

A MIDCOM session is a lasting association, not necessarily a TCP connection. The RFC explicitly says the MIDCOM protocol is yet to be devised; it describes the architecture and protocol requirements rather than message formats.
sections.plainLanguage: An agent registers first, then starts a session with a middlebox and makes requests during that session. This RFC describes the arrangement but does not define the protocol messages.

sections.title: A SIP Call Through a Middlebox
sections.content:
The example places a MIDCOM agent on a SIP proxy. The agent reads the Session Description Protocol information in SIP messages to learn the dynamic ports for RTP and RTCP media traffic.

For a firewall, the agent asks permission for media flows before relaying the invitation, so early media can pass. For NAPT, it asks the middlebox to create port bindings and session descriptors, then updates SDP with the translated port. With both NAT and firewall services, NAT operations precede firewall operations in the example.
sections.plainLanguage: The SIP proxy learns which ports a call will use and asks the middlebox to allow those flows. When NAT is involved, the proxy also updates the call's port information.

sections.title: Deployment, Scope, and Security
sections.content:
The RFC suggests notifications for events such as session termination and timers so that middleboxes can recover dynamic resources if an agent disappears. Its applicability statement focuses on a single firewall or NAT middlebox in a DMZ at the edge of a private domain. Discovery and communication among middleboxes are outside its scope.

Agent-middlebox communication needs authentication, integrity, and replay protection; confidentiality may also be needed. The RFC points to existing mechanisms such as IPsec and TLS, and warns that an attacker impersonating an agent could request changes to firewall or NAT state.
sections.plainLanguage: Middleboxes should clean up resources when agents fail and should authenticate requests. The framework focuses on one edge middlebox, not discovery or coordination among several middleboxes.
